title: Fractional & Small Interests
metaTitle: Fractional Mineral Interests - Sell in Michigan
metaDescription: Own a 1/16th, 1/32nd, or smaller mineral interest in Michigan? Find out if that fractional Antrim share is actually worth selling before you write it off.
heroLead: A 1/64th interest in a well up in Otsego County sounds like nothing until you actually check what it's throwing off, and by then most owners have already decided it's not worth the paperwork.
intro: Michigan's Antrim boom in the eighties and nineties spread ownership across families the same way most old plays do: land gets passed down, minerals get split among heirs, and three generations later a great-grandkid in another state owns a fraction of a fraction of an original tract. It's not unusual to see interests down at 1/32nd, 1/64th, even smaller, tied to a well that's been producing since before the current owner was born. A lot of these owners have never sold because the checks are small enough that nobody's bothered to look closer, or because they assume a fractional interest that tiny can't possibly be worth the effort to sell.

Sometimes that assumption is right. A dust-dry fractional share of a nearly depleted well genuinely might not be worth much. But sometimes it's wrong, and the only way to know is to actually look at recent production, confirm the exact fraction you hold against the county record, and get a real number instead of guessing based on how small the check looks on paper.

sections.heading: Why Small Doesn't Mean Worthless
paragraphs: The size of your fraction and the value of your interest aren't the same thing. A 1/64th interest in a strong producing unit can be worth more than a 1/4 interest in a well that's basically stripper production at this point. What actually drives value is the well's current production, how many net mineral acres your fraction represents, remaining reserves, and who's operating the unit. Owners get hung up on the fraction itself as if it's the whole story, when it's really just one input into a bigger calculation.

sections.heading: The Paperwork Problem Fractional Owners Face
paragraphs: Small interests carry outsized paperwork burden relative to what they pay out. You still get a 1099 every year no matter how small the check is. You still need to keep the operator updated if you move, or the checks stop and end up in state unclaimed property instead of your mailbox. If there are multiple heirs holding pieces of the same original interest, someone has to coordinate updates, changes of address, and eventually another round of division when an heir passes and their share splits again. For a lot of owners, the administrative weight of a tiny interest outweighs what it actually pays, and that's a legitimate reason to consider selling separate from whatever the raw dollar value comes out to.

sections.heading: Confirming What You Actually Own
paragraphs: Before pricing anything, we confirm the legal description and your exact fractional share against the county register of deeds record in whichever Michigan county the minerals sit in. Old family paperwork sometimes lists a fraction that doesn't match the current recorded interest, especially after multiple generations of heirship and probate. It's common to find that what a family believed was a 1/16th interest is actually smaller after later generations split it further, or occasionally larger if a sibling's share reverted. Getting that number right matters because it's the multiplier on everything else in the valuation.

This is also where we catch interests that are producing but the owner never realized it, because the checks were going to an old address or a deceased relative's name and got redirected to state unclaimed property instead of the current heir. If you inherited a fractional interest and have never seen a check, that's worth checking before assuming the interest is dry.

faqs.question: Is a 1/64th mineral interest even worth selling?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on what that fraction represents in current production and net mineral acres, not the fraction itself. Some small interests in active units are worth real money. Others in depleted wells aren't. The only way to know is to check recent production against your confirmed share.

faqs.question: How do I find out my exact fractional share?
faqs.answer: Start with the county register of deeds in the Michigan county where the minerals are located, cross-referenced against any division order the operator sent you. Family paperwork passed down through heirs isn't always accurate after multiple generations of splitting.

faqs.question: Why haven't I ever received a royalty check on my interest?
faqs.answer: A few common reasons: the well isn't currently producing, your address was never updated with the operator after you inherited, or your share was too small to trigger a check under the operator's minimum payment threshold and is accruing or sitting with the state as unclaimed property.

faqs.question: Does it cost anything to find out what my fractional interest is worth?
faqs.answer: No. We review your documentation and recent production history and give you a straight answer, and there's no obligation to sell if the number or the situation doesn't work for you.

faqs.question: Can I sell my fractional interest without the other heirs agreeing?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. A fractional undivided interest is generally your own to sell regardless of what co-owning heirs decide to do with their shares, though it's worth checking your specific deed or estate paperwork for any unusual restrictions before assuming that's the case for you.
